prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions amplify and propagate shocks into credit cycles and macroeconomic fluctuations

statement.case_for: The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is a single, well-defined discovery. Collateral values and credit limits feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. The idea has been tested over roughly three decades, including by the 2007-09 crisis and the work that followed, and it is now standard in macro-financial and central-bank modelling. This also meets the criterion I value most: a mechanism that explains why a pattern arises, not just that it exists. The work is mature, so timing is not a concern. I keep Gertler in the trio because his contributions to financial intermediation and to the quantitative use of financial frictions in policy analysis (including work with Kiyotaki) extend the mechanism beyond the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. I take this from background knowledge, not from verified citation data.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic and attributional overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. Part of the accelerator credit sits with an existing laureate, so Gertler's share is the weakest link in the trio. The empirical identification of collateral channels is also less clean than the theory. Several members rank B023 or B047 higher on breadth of application or on how clearly credit can be assigned.

responses.point: Hassler proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues that Gertler and Gilchrist build on Bernanke-Gertler, that Bernanke's 2022 prize already covers part of the banking and crisis side, and that two names are the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I take this seriously. Kiyotaki-Moore is the core, and a two-name prize would be fully defensible and probably the safest on attribution. I still keep Gertler for two reasons. His work on financial intermediation and on the quantitative use of financial frictions in policy models is not obviously the part Bernanke's 2022 prize covered. And a prize limited to the 1997 model would miss how the idea became usable for policy analysis. I would not fight a two-name outcome if the committee judges Gertler's independent share too uncertain. The question is whether his post-accelerator work is a distinct achievement or an extension of an already-honoured one.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B006 second behind B023. He values the collateral-constraint mechanism but worries about overlap with the 2022 prize and about Gertler's recognition being split with the New Keynesian ballot.
responses.response: The split is real, but I think it cuts toward including Gertler here. B048 has diffuse credit across eight names with no clean trio, and Gertler is unlikely to be recognised there. His case rests on the financial-frictions work, which fits the B006 frame. On B023 I agree it is highly influential. For me the attribution problem across the technology and trade strands is larger. Autor, Katz and Hanson belong to partly separate discoveries, and the three-name limit forces a compromise there that it does not force here.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B047 first. His case is that BLP and the dynamic-industry work turned industrial organisation into a quantitative field, that the field has had no recent recognition, and that Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is the cleanest credit allocation. He ranks B006 third because the accelerator strand overlaps with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I accept that B047 has the sharper attribution. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core is compact and mature, and the method is widely applied. I did not rank it in my opening top eight, and I should say that this partly reflects my own distance from IO. I should not let that discount the case. Where I differ is that B006 is also a foundational mechanism with a well-bounded origin in Kiyotaki-Moore. The overlap with 2022 concerns the banking-crisis lineage, and the collateral-amplification mechanism is not the same discovery. I would like to know from the IO specialists how large the omitted Bresnahan-Reiss contribution is, since that determines how clean the trio really is.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B031 third and B006 eighth. She regards the mobility work as strong in measurement and identification but somewhat early, and she is concerned about overlap between B006 and both the 2022 prize and Bernanke's accelerator work.
responses.response: I ranked B031 second because building population-scale data and then testing mechanisms rigorously is a method I admire. I accept your maturity point and have lowered its priority for that reason. Causal claims on place effects are still being tested. On B006, I agree that the accelerator overlap is the main weakness, and that is why I treat Gertler's inclusion as the open question and not Kiyotaki and Moore. The collateral-cycle mechanism itself is not covered by earlier prizes.

uncertainties: Whether Gertler's independent contribution beyond the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator is large enough to justify a third name, or whether Kiyotaki and Moore alone is the safer attribution.
How much weight the committee gives to thematic proximity to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether the compactness of the B047 attribution outweighs the broader foundational reach of B006; I cannot settle this from the opening statements alone.
My knowledge of citation counts and the empirical record on collateral channels is from general background and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore or Gertler is documented. My Lund colleague Tommy Andersson ranks B006 third, and I note the shared affiliation only for completeness.
